Given the brevity of this article, and how largely self-contained the narrative here is, I feel that an in-line link is the way to go, to avoid the potential of such a link coming across as forced. In the third paragraph of the description, the article mentions String-17 being sent back by a duly-authorized agent of the Foundation. Members of the Temporal Anomalies Department would likely be such authorized agents. As such, I am proposing the following edit:

Changing the following:

String 17 was detected [DATA REDACTED] ten years after the object's construction. It consists of 347 characters, either heavily encrypted or [DATA REDACTED]. Within the first fifty characters, however, is sufficient data to establish ███████████ (p █ █████) that it will be sent by a duly-authorized agent of the SCP Foundation. Its date of origin is unknown: to date, it has not yet been sent.

To this:

String 17 was detected [DATA REDACTED] ten years after the object's construction. It consists of 347 characters, either heavily encrypted or [DATA REDACTED]. Within the first fifty characters, however, is sufficient data to establish ███████████ (p █ █████) that it will be sent by a duly-authorized agent of the SCP Foundation. Its date of origin is unknown: to date, it has not yet been sent.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.content:encoded: It sends messages into the past using science. The Foundation made it. They've received a message that they don't remember sending, and they're pretty sure it's from a Foundation member. Thus, they are guaranteed that the Foundation will exist at least long enough for that message to be sent, but it is not guaranteed that they will last longer. As such, their policy is to do whatever they can to prevent the message from being sent, because they will continue to exist so long as it is not sent.

item.content:encoded:
I don't think there's enough hints that String 17 is just noise to keep the idea. The probability is so vanishingly small that the machine would have to receive many, many more strings for there to be even a chance of noise resembling an actual message. Fifty random characters, even just in ASCII, has a 1 in approximately 2.3*10^105 chance of occurring (not counting error correction bits etc, and it's much worse with UTF-8). Too slim a chance, unless the machine is receiving constantly for a very long time.

Besides that, I still don't think there's enough inherent reason to send it at all for the Foundation to be tempted. I think perhaps you could put in something about scenarios where the Foundation may not survive, but some of humanity might, and so the message would be sent to save the remnants from any paradox. That way there's a tension in every crisis, the faith of String 17 clashing against persistent doubt in the Foundation's odds of survival.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I like this, I appreciate the logic behind it, but tentatively agree with those who dislike the degree of expungement. There's not quite enough to indicate that it's likely to simply be noise (mentioned as the likely case upthread), and not nearly enough to get any sense of why String 17 would ever be sent in the first place if it were intentionally sent. Containing the message to get "paradox insurance" is all well and good, but there has to be a better indication to the reader of the possible motivations for sending the message at all. A warning? A rogue agent? The Foundation succumbing to despair and cancelling its insurance policy?

Compare with SCP-699, which a) is implied to be sent from an alternate timeline, thus sidestepping paradox concerns, and b) was explicitly sent somewhere/somewhen incapable of opening it, and at the very last minute as a desperation measure. SCP-711 doesn't quite have the same raison-d'etre, since the message description is too heavily redacted (possibly because the Foundation hasn't even fully decrypted it) to give a compelling motivation for sending the message during a given crisis.

My suggestion would be to at least hint at a circumstance where sending the message would be approved - say, when the Foundation is under just the right degree of threat, such that survival is unlikely but possible, and the odds of not being able to send the message at all (with the attendant paradox) are high enough that the crisis at hand becomes the lesser danger.

And personally, I'd have the message consist only of its criteria for sending. Not the specific crisis which triggered (will trigger) it, merely the condition(s) to select the point of sending.

item.content:encoded:
Everything you say assumes unchanging paradox-free timeline. This is… quite an assumption.
I think I'll just give a few examples of how this all can go horribly wrong, to make my point clearer.

changeable timeline (best-case scenario):

  • Foundation doesn't send String 17. Ever. Nothing bad happens. Foundation spends insane amount of resources for hundreds of years guarding worthless piece of junk.

unchanging paradox-free timeline (your scenario):

  • Foundation sends String 17. Than everybody dies. 711 is completely useless to save anyone.
  • Chaos Insurgency steals 711, brainwashes Foundation agent to send String 17.
  • Earthquake smashes Storage Site-██ to pieces, lighting strikes exposed pieces of 711, sending String 17.

unchangeable paradox-resistant timeline:

  • Foundation attempts to send String 17, but string received doesn't much the first version. Time between receiving and sending repeats slightly differently. And repeats. And repeats. And repeats. After couple billion cycles, strings in two subsequent iterations matches. Timeline restores itself. Than everybody dies. 711 is completely useless to save anyone.
  • Foundation attempts to send String 17, but string received doesn't much the first version. Time loops on itself in attempt to resolve the paradox. Everything after the moment of sending String 17 ceases to exist.

unchangeable paradox-vulnerable timeline:

  • Foundation tries to to prevent sending of String 17 in order to prolong its existence. String 17 is not send when it should have been. Paradox is born. All that was, is or should have been ceases to exist.

Paradoxes are dangerous, unpredictable and scary. There is no way to tell what type of timeline you live in until it's too late. This is why 196 is Keter level object. This is why preventing paradoxes at all costs is number one priority when dealing with time-related phenomena.

To try to create and use paradox for your advantage… Well there are easier ways to cause K class event.

Actually, I was going somewhere slightly different with all the expungement, etc.: I'm trying to imply that there's a pretty darn good chance that String 17 is just line noise. We might be expending all this effort on something that hasn't worked since it was first tested. Clearly, I've failed to get that point across; it was meant to be half the article's hook. :/

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
The reason not to send String 17 is that, since we know a Foundation agent sent it, we know that the Foundation is guaranteed to survive til it's sent. No crisis can kill us: we will be around, in some form, to send String 17.

We also know that String 17 is guaranteed to be sent. If we destroy 711, well, it's is still going to be sent; that's what a predestination paradox is. All we'd do by destroying 17 is guarantee that we have no control over when or how it's sent, or by what or whom. We break the thing? Okay; now we've ensured that the plans will leak, that some other faction will build a new 711, and the Foundation will — someday, somehow — be reduced to such impotent tatters that its last surviving agents give up and send the message. If we keep 711 around, we can at least do everything in our power to postpone that day.

And yeah, it might be the case that the plans'll leak, etc., etc. no matter what we do. But if there's a chance, however small, that we can postpone it… Well, it's not like the Foundation to give up even the smallest chance.

Does that clarify matters any? If so, any suggestions on how I can work it into the article proper?
